meta.case_name: Bank Savings for Savings Bank CIO

prompt.context: Our client is the CIO of a large domestic bank. He's been tasked to cut $100 million of costs within 9 months.
prompt.question: Is cutting $100M in costs within 9 months feasible without disrupting service?

clarifying_info.q: What counts as a service disruption?
clarifying_info.a: Service disruption means any noticeable alteration to how customers interact with the bank.

clarifying_info.q: What does the CIO's office do?
clarifying_info.a: The office of the CIO supports internal and external information organization and access — it manages internal systems that allow employees such as clerks to view customer accounts, and manages external systems such as online banking that allow customers to view accounts.

exhibits.title: Total Annual Costs
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of the CIO office's total annual cost base by category
exhibits.data: Total annual costs = $3 billion; cost categories include Maintenance, Help Desk, and other buckets (exact proportions shown in chart)

framework: Narrow focus on cost — identify all cost categories under the CIO's purview
Assess size of each cost bucket relative to the $100M target
Evaluate feasibility of cuts in each bucket without service disruption
Consider labor vs. non-labor costs within each category
Consider build/buy/outsource options (domestic vs. international suppliers)
Assess timeline: can savings be realized within 9 months (accounting for severance and transition)?

questions.prompt: Question 1: We are considering two plans to cut costs associated with Maintenance. Labor costs make up 80% of Maintenance costs and we can replace half of the existing maintenance labor force either with a domestic 3rd-party supplier ($45/hour) or an international 3rd-party supplier ($18/hour). In either case, we must pay severance equal to 3 months of wages to the employees we let go. What are the savings associated with each plan over the 9-month period?
questions.guidance: Candidate should extract Maintenance costs from Exhibit 1, calculate current labor cost for the half being replaced, compute cost of new supplier labor for the remaining 6 months (after 3-month severance period), subtract severance and new labor cost from old labor cost, and compare domestic vs. international options. Strong candidates will note that cost of new labor should be based on hours worked, not headcount, and will handle the 9-month vs. 3-month severance offset cleanly.

math.setup: From Exhibit 1: read Maintenance as a share of $3B total annual costs. Labor = 80% of Maintenance costs. Half the labor force is replaced. Severance = 3 months wages. New labor operates for remaining 6 months. Current labor hourly rate implied from existing cost base. New labor rates: domestic $45/hr, international $18/hr. The casebook notes: cost of new labor calculated as (3.2 - 0.8) * new labor hourly rate (implying hours in millions), yielding savings of $36M (domestic) and $101M (international) over 9 months.
steps: Identify Maintenance labor cost from Exhibit 1 for the half of the workforce being replaced
Calculate severance cost = 3 months of those wages
Calculate new supplier cost for 6 months at $45/hr (domestic) or $18/hr (international)
Savings = old labor cost over 9 months - severance - new supplier cost over 6 months
math.answer: Domestic 3rd-party supplier: ~$36M savings over 9 months. International 3rd-party supplier: ~$101M savings over 9 months.

questions.prompt: Question 2: The international supplier looks promising. What else should we consider?
questions.guidance: Candidate should raise qualitative risks and considerations for outsourcing to an international supplier, particularly in a banking context. Strong answers will cover: (1) service disruption risk from quality or communication gaps with an international vendor; (2) regulatory and legal concerns around outsourcing sensitive banking data and systems to an offshore entity; (3) data security and privacy; (4) transition / knowledge-transfer risk; (5) contract flexibility and ability to reverse course.

questions.prompt: Question 3: What are some ways to think about cost savings in the Help Desk?
questions.guidance: This is a brainstorming question. Strong candidates will generate multiple distinct levers: (1) outsourcing similar to maintenance (domestic vs. international, with same regulatory caveats); (2) staffing schedule optimization — identifying and eliminating overstaffing relative to demand patterns (peak/off-peak); (3) segmenting Help Desk staff by issue type so common or simple issues are handled by lower-cost specialists or automated self-service options, reserving expensive staff for complex issues. Candidates should consider both labor and non-labor dimensions.

questions.prompt: Question 4: What would you recommend to our client?
questions.guidance: Candidate should lead with a clear 'answer-first' recommendation, supported by quantified factors. A strong recommendation: pursue the international outsourcing of half the Maintenance labor force (saving ~$101M vs. the $100M target), while managing regulatory risk through legal review and phased transition. Key elements: (1) bottom-line recommendation up front; (2) 2-3 supporting factors with numbers; (3) explicit risks to the recommendation; (4) concrete next steps.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways to think about cost savings in the Help Desk?

categories.name: Outsourcing
ideas: International 3rd-party supplier (higher savings, higher regulatory/quality risk)

categories.name: Staffing Optimization
ideas: Analyze demand patterns to identify overstaffed periods
Reduce headcount or hours during off-peak windows
Use part-time or flexible staffing to match demand

categories.name: Service Segmentation
ideas: Segment issues by complexity — route common/simple issues to lower-cost specialists
Invest in self-service options (FAQs, automated chat) to deflect low-value calls
Create tiered support so high-cost staff handle only complex issues

recommendation: Pursue international outsourcing of half the Maintenance labor force, projected to save ~$101M over 9 months, meeting the $100M target
Complement with Help Desk optimizations (staffing schedules and self-service) to create a cost buffer and reduce execution risk
risks: Regulatory and legal exposure from offshoring sensitive banking systems and data
Service disruption risk if the international supplier's quality or communication falls below current standards
Transition risk: knowledge transfer and ramp-up time may compress the effective savings window within 9 months
next_steps: Conduct legal and regulatory review of international outsourcing constraints for a domestic bank
Issue RFP and due-diligence process for international supplier candidates
Model Help Desk demand patterns to quantify staffing optimization opportunity
Define service-level agreements and quality metrics to protect against service disruption
